topic: The Early Church: The Church in Acts
subject: religious-studies

items.title: The earliest Christians thought Jesus would return within their lifetime
items.claim: Paul's letters (50s CE) are the oldest Christian texts. What does he tell his churches about the timing of Christ's return?

options.text: He explicitly warns that it will be many centuries away
He tells believers — in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 — that 'we who are alive, who are left' will be caught up to meet the Lord
He refuses to discuss the timing at all
He places the return precisely at AD 70, the destruction of the Temple

items.reveal:
1 Thessalonians 4:15-17, written around 50-51 CE, includes Paul among those still alive at the Parousia. 1 Corinthians 7:29 says 'the appointed time has grown short.' Mark 9:1 has Jesus saying 'some standing here will not taste death' before seeing the Kingdom.

When Christ did not return, later texts (e.g. 2 Peter 3:8 — 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years') reinterpret the delay. This shift is one of the central transformations of early Christian theology.
items.why: Treating the New Testament as a unified, settled doctrine misses that it documents a community reinterpreting itself in real time. The 'delay of the Parousia' is one of the formative pressures on Christian thought.

items.title: British religious affiliation has dropped sharply since the 1960s
items.claim: What does the 2021 UK Census show about religion?

options.text: For the first time, less than half of England and Wales (46.2%) identified as Christian; 37.2% had no religion; Islam grew to 6.5%; Hindu, Sikh, Jewish, Buddhist and Other religions made up the remainder
All religions are at the same percentage

items.reveal:
The 2001 Census recorded 72% Christian; 2011 recorded 59%; 2021 recorded 46% in England and Wales. The 'no religion' category rose from 15% (2001) to 25% (2011) to 37% (2021). Scotland (2022 census) showed similar trends; Northern Ireland remains more religious.

Muslim population: 3% (2001), 5% (2011), 6.5% (2021).

Secularisation theory (Bryan Wilson, Peter Berger) predicted declining religious influence with modernity. The reality has been more complex — declining institutional affiliation alongside persistent or growing 'spiritual but not religious' identification and increasing pluralism.
items.why: British religion is restructured, not just declining. The Census numbers show a more religiously plural country where institutional Christianity has lost its majority position — major implications for education, ethics and public life.

items.title: Wittgenstein's later work treated religious language as a 'language game'
items.claim: How did the later Wittgenstein approach religious language?

options.text: He argued religious language is meaningless

Religious language is a 'language game' embedded in a 'form of life' — it has its own grammar and logic, not reducible to scientific or empirical assertion. It is meaningful within its practice, regardless of whether it asserts external facts
He defended a literal cognitive interpretation
He treated all language games as equally true

items.reveal:
Wittgenstein's 'Philosophical Investigations' (published 1953) replaced the picture theory of meaning from his earlier 'Tractatus' (1921) with a use-theory. 'The meaning of a word is its use in the language.'

Religious language games — prayer, worship, doctrinal assertion — function differently from scientific language games. D.Z. Phillips and Norman Malcolm developed Wittgensteinian philosophy of religion in the 20th century.

Critics (Antony Flew, 'Theology and Falsification' 1950) argued this 'reduces' religious claims to non-cognitive expressions — but Wittgenstein himself was more nuanced, refusing both literalist and reductionist readings.
items.why: The 20th-century philosophy of religion shifted from 'do these claims correspond to reality?' to 'what kind of claims are these?'. Wittgenstein's move opens space for religious practice without requiring scientific-style verification.
